html:
The Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, or Central African Federation, joined three British territories in southern Africa from 1953 to 1963: the self-governing colony of Southern Rhodesia and the protectorates of Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland.

White settlers, led from Southern Rhodesia, wanted to join the copper wealth of the north with the farms and industry of the south and to keep power out of African hands. Britain backed it as a way to build a strong economy and a counterweight to apartheid South Africa, with talk of "partnership" between the races. Africans in the north opposed it from the start, fearing rule by Southern Rhodesia's settlers. Its capital was Salisbury, now Harare, and its best-known project was the Kariba Dam on the Zambezi, whose power went to the copper mines.

African nationalist movements grew fast against it. Hastings Banda led the struggle in Nyasaland, where a state of emergency in 1959 left dozens dead, and Kenneth Kaunda led it in Northern Rhodesia. A British commission in 1960 reported that African opposition was deep and widespread, and that the territories should be able to leave. Britain let the two northern territories leave, and the federation ended at the close of 1963. In 1964 Nyasaland became Malawi and Northern Rhodesia became Zambia. Southern Rhodesia, left alone under white rule, declared independence in 1965 as Rhodesia.
